raw_case_text:
A 62-year-old male patient was admitted with after the onset of fever with chills and rigor lasting for 5 days. The sensorium was reportedly altered since the day before admission. He had no headache, vomiting, jaundice, seizure or any weakness. He was neither diabetic nor hypertensive. There was no history of any other recent illness or vaccination.
Physical examination revealed that he was febrile (103 F), tachycardic (pulse rate - 124/min), normotensive (blood pressure [BP] - 110/70), and tachypneic (respiratory rate - 36/min). Neurologic examination showed drowsiness without any focal neurological deficit or meningeal signs. Plantar response was extensor bilaterally. Clinical examinations of respiratory, cardiovascular, and abdominal systems revealed no abnormality.
Full blood count revealed a normocytic anemia (hemoglobin - 10.4 g/dl, mean corpuscular volume - 82 fl), and erythrocytic sedimentation rate (ESR) was 38 mm in 1sth (Westergren method). Thick and thin blood smears were prepared which showed ring forms of Plasmodium falciparum and immunochromatographic test for P. falciparum histidine-rich protein 2 (PfHRP-2)-based assay (ICT, Access Bio. Inc., NJ, USA) was strongly positive. Blood tests revealed impaired renal functions (serum urea - 85 mg/dl and serum creatinine - 2.4 mg/dl), whereas liver function tests (LFTs) and electrolytes were normal. Hence, a diagnosis of severe falciparum malaria with cerebral manifestations and renal failure was made and a treatment with intravenous artesunate was initiated at the dose of 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12, and 24 h, then once daily. He also underwent hemodialysis once and started improving on the 3rd day. A clear clinical improvement was shown upon treatment, until he became fully conscious and ambulant on day 4.
On day 5 (10 days after the onset of fever), he developed weakness of lower limbs first and then upper limbs, which progressively worsened over the next 3 days, making the patient bed-ridden eventually. Neurologic examination was performed. Higher functions were maintained; cranial nerve functions were intact; a lower motor type of quadriparesis was shown. Muscle strength was reduced to 2/5 in lower limbs and 3/5 in upper limbs. There was hypotonia, but no fasciculations were detected. All deep tendon reflexes were absent. Plantar responses were flexor bilaterally. Nerve conduction studies of both common peroneal and posterior tibial nerves showed prolonged distal latencies, grossly diminished amplitudes and velocities. Sensory nerve conduction in both upper and lower limbs was absent. F-wave latencies were diminished in both upper and lower limbs. These findings were suggestive of mixed demyelinating and axonal neuropathy involving both motor and sensory nerves and radiculopathy-consistent with a diagnosis of Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS). A study of the cerebrospinal fluid revealed no cells, but a protein content of 500 mg%, confirming the diagnosis of GBS. As the patient could not afford intravenous immunoglobulin and plasmapheresis, he was not given any specific treatment. He did not have further progression of weakness and respiratory muscles or facial nerve was not involved. He improved gradually and was discharged 22 days later (day 27) when his muscle strength was 4/5 in all four limbs.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 62-year-old male presenting with a 5-day history of high-grade fever with chills, tachypnea, and altered sensorium, followed post-recovery by acute ascending quadriparesis.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with fever accompanied by chills and rigors for 5 days, progressing to acute drowsiness and confusion 1 day prior to admission. Physical examination showed tachycardia, tachypnea, and extensor plantars, with laboratory findings of acute renal impairment and anemia. He was treated with intravenous artesunate and temporary hemodialysis, achieving full consciousness and ambulation by hospital day 4. However, on day 5, he developed rapidly progressive ascending weakness starting in the lower extremities and involving the upper extremities over 3 days, rendering him quadriparetic and bedridden.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy; non-diabetic, non-hypertensive. No recent prior illness or vaccination.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, chills, rigors, drowsiness, and progressive symmetric quadriparesis. Negative for headache, vomiting, jaundice, seizures, or sensory loss. Medications and allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature: 103 F, heart rate: 124 beats/min, blood pressure: 110/70 mmHg, respiratory rate: 36 breaths/min. Drowsy on admission, bilateral extensor plantar responses; cardiovascular, respiratory, and abdominal examinations were normal. Day 5 neurologic exam: Symmetrical flaccid quadriparesis (muscle power grade 2/5 in lower limbs, 3/5 in upper limbs), generalized hypotonia, generalized areflexia (absent deep tendon reflexes), and bilateral flexor plantar responses. Sensory examination intact; no cranial nerve palsies or autonomic instability.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: Hemoglobin: 10.4 g/dL, MCV: 82 fL (normocytic anemia), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR): 38 mm in 1st hour. Serum urea: 85 mg/dL, serum creatinine: 2.4 mg/dL. Liver function tests and serum electrolytes: Within normal limits.
objective.advanced_workup: Lumbar puncture / CSF analysis: Total cell count: 2 cells/mm3, CSF protein: 140 mg/dL (demonstrating albuminocytological dissociation). Nerve conduction velocity (NCV) / electromyography: Marked slowing of conduction velocities, prolonged distal latencies, and conduction blocks consistent with acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (AIDP / Guillain-Barre syndrome).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria complicated by acute kidney injury and post-infectious acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (Guillain-Barre syndrome / AIDP).
Diagnostic confirmation: Thick and thin blood smears demonstrated ring forms of Plasmodium falciparum; immunochromatographic test for PfHRP-2 was strongly positive. Post-malaria GBS was confirmed by classic albuminocytological dissociation on CSF analysis and demyelinating features on electrodiagnostic testing.
Plan & Outcome: Initial falciparum malaria and acute renal failure treated with intravenous artesunate (2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12, 24 hours, then daily) and a single session of hemodialysis, with complete defervescence and parasite clearance. Following onset of Guillain-Barre syndrome, treated with intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG, 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days). Muscle power improved progressively, and the patient regained independent ambulation with support at 4-week follow-up.
